title: Peripheral Device Enumeration via System Utilities and API Calls
shortTitle: Peripheral Device Enumeration via System Utilities and AP...
summary: Peripheral device enumeration is the step in which an operator lists attached hardware, such as removable drives, cameras, keyboards and printers, to find devices that can carry data out or reveal where the host is used. The detection collects process creation for the command line utilities that report plug and play devices, PowerShell script block records of the device cmdlets, and the setup interface activity that those utilities generate, then looks for enumeration from scripting hosts, office documents, or user accounts on hosts that never perform that task. The technique is quiet and the commands are legitimate, so the rule is deliberately low severity and earns its value through baselining rather than through blocking.

beginner.definition: Peripheral devices are the hardware attached to a computer, such as a memory stick, a camera or a printer. This plan looks for commands that list those devices. Attackers use the list to find ways to copy data out. The detection checks who ran the list and from which program.
beginner.whyItMatters: A device list tells an attacker whether a memory stick will work and what hardware is present. It also hints at how a host is used. A laptop with a camera is not the same as a server. The commands are normal tools, so you cannot block them without breaking support work. Watching the context still gives you a useful early signal. It also helps you spot a host that suddenly shows interest in hardware it never uses.
howItWorks: The endpoint agent records process creation with the full command line for the device listing tools.
PowerShell script block logging captures the device related cmdlets when a script runs them.
The rule notes the parent process, because a document reader listing devices is unexpected.
It also collects access to the registry area where plug and play device records are stored.
The host is compared with a baseline of which machines normally query hardware.
Enumeration from a scripting host on a server, or by an unusual account, is raised for review.
beginner.example: Think of a courier who walks into an office. Instead of delivering a parcel, they count the lockers and note which ones are open. Counting is not stealing, but it is preparation. Staff would notice because couriers in that building never walk the corridors. In the same way, a server has no reason to list hardware. So the interest itself is the clue.
takeaways: Device listing commands are legitimate, so context and baselines carry the detection.
The parent process tells you whether the query belongs on that host.
Peripheral discovery is often preparation for taking data out of the network.

objectives: Name the common commands and cmdlets that list plug and play devices.
Explain why peripheral discovery precedes data theft in many intrusions.
Use the parent process to judge whether a device query is expected.
Describe how to baseline which hosts normally enumerate hardware.
Explain why this detection is intentionally low severity.
dataSources: Sysmon event 1 process creation showing device listing utilities with parent image and command line
PowerShell script block logging event 4104 capturing the plug and play device cmdlets that were run
Windows Security event 4663 object access on the registry keys that store device installation records
Windows device installation event log entries that record driver and hardware records on the host
logic: The detection identifies the small set of commands and script calls that enumerate attached hardware, such as the management interface query for plug and play entities, the command line device utility with an enumeration switch, and the PowerShell cmdlets that return device information. Because these tools are shipped with the operating system and used by support staff, the rule scores context instead: whether the parent process is a scripting host, an office application or a web service, whether the account is an interactive user on a server that has no hardware to manage, whether the same host queried devices several times in a short period, and whether the query came with other discovery commands such as system or network listing. The malicious case is a burst of hardware and system enumeration by an unfamiliar parent on a host whose baseline contains no device queries, which is why command line, parent image, account and host role must be read together.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Peripheral Device Enumeration From A Scripting Parent
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection:
#     CommandLine|contains:
#       - 'Win32_PnPEntity'
#       - 'Get-PnpDevice'
#       - 'pnputil /enum-devices'
#   filter:
#     ParentImage|endswith:
#       - '\services.exe'
#       - '\ccmexec.exe'
#     User|endswith: '$'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: low
falsePositives: Hardware inventory agents that enumerate attached devices as part of an asset management scan
Help desk scripts that list printers, cameras or docking stations while solving a support ticket
Device driver installation tools that query existing hardware before installing a new driver
Imaging and provisioning workflows that record the hardware of a newly built machine
tuningNotes: Baseline the hardware inventory tooling and the accounts it runs under, then exclude those combinations rather than the command names, because the same commands are useful to attackers. Scope the rule to servers and to hosts in the finance and research groups where hardware enumeration has no business purpose. That narrowing keeps the queue almost empty but hides discovery on general user workstations, so leave a lower severity version running estate wide and review it with the other discovery signals during triage.
